title: How lovely are thy tabernacles (Psalm 83 [84])
hook: even the sparrow finds a home near the altar
tomorrow: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 89 [90])

segments.voice: Yesterday, my soul thirsteth, the morning psalm. Your line was early I seek you. Did the phone wait this morning? Today, a psalm about a place. Day one hundred seventy-three.

Walk into an old stone church on a weekday afternoon, and look up. Sometimes there's a bird up there. A sparrow that flew in through an open door and now lives in the rafters, hopping along a beam above the altar, completely unbothered by the saints and the candles. People smile at it. The sexton sighs about it. Long ago, a pilgrim walking into the Temple in Jerusalem noticed the same thing, a small bird nesting near the altar, and felt a stab of envy.
screen: `AN OLD STONE CHURCH.` → `A SPARROW IN THE RAFTERS.` → `A PILGRIM'S ENVY.`

segments.voice: Psalm 83 in the Douay, 84 in most Bibles, is a pilgrim's song. It opens: "How lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! my soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord." Tabernacles here means dwellings, the courts of the Temple. Fainteth: homesick to the point of weakness. Then the bird. "For the sparrow hath found herself a house, and the turtle a nest for herself where she may lay her young ones: Thy altars, O Lord of hosts." The turtle is a turtledove. Two of the smallest, cheapest birds there are, and they get to live at the altar full time, while the pilgrim can only visit. It's funny and it's aching at once. Then the road there. Blessed are those whose strength is in you, the psalm says, who have set their hearts on the journey, and it names a valley they pass through. The Hebrew is the valley of Baca, a place name nobody can locate for sure; it may mean balsam trees, or weeping. The Latin read it as weeping, and so the Douay says: "In the vale of tears." That's where the phrase comes from. It's the same vale of tears Catholics sigh through in the Hail, Holy Queen. And the pilgrims go through it, the psalm says, and make it a place of springs. Then the famous line: "For better is one day in thy courts above thousands." One day near God, better than a thousand anywhere else. Brahms set the opening of this psalm in his German Requiem: a song about going home, sung for the dead.
screen: `MY SOUL LONGETH AND FAINTETH.` · `THE SPARROW FOUND A HOUSE.` · `THROUGH THE VALE OF TEARS.` · `ONE DAY ABOVE THOUSANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in a church or a quiet room. If there's a church nearby, stop in sometime today and just sit. For now, find the quietest corner you can, even a parked car. Settle, and breathe. Picture the sparrow on the beam, completely at home. Ask yourself where you feel that at home, and when you last were there. If you pray, you can say, how lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord. If you don't, let this quiet corner be a small place to rest. The bell holds the time.
How lovely are thy tabernacles. A pilgrim's homesick song for God's house, where even the sparrow has a home. Today's word.
screen: `HOW LOVELY ARE THY TABERNACLES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the sparrow found a home. Today, look for one small bird, and let it remind you where you belong. Day one hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 83 [84] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Mass, often on feasts of dedication of churches; many make short visits to a church simply to sit in the quiet.

original.note: Hebrew: how lovely, how beloved, the psalm's opening words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about pretty churches.
what it means: a pilgrim homesick for God's house, envying the sparrow, walking through the vale of tears.
what a scholar hears: the valley of Baca may mean balsam trees or weeping; the Latin chose weeping, giving us vale of tears, which the Salve Regina echoes.

notes: Douay Psalm 83 wording (verses 2, 4, 7, 11): confirm against a Challoner edition.
Valley of Baca: meaning uncertain (balsam/baca shrubs, or weeping); Vulgate 'in valle lacrimarum'. The Salve Regina's 'in hac lacrimarum valle' echoes this phrase. Confirm link.
Brahms, German Requiem, 4th movement 'Wie lieblich sind deine Wohnungen' sets Psalm 84:1–2, 4. Confirm.
Hebrew opening mah-yedidot (how lovely/beloved). Confirm pointing.
